paragraphs: “Damn it all!” Ivan cried, his face twisting with anger. “Why are you always in such a panic about your life? All my brother Dmitri’s threats are just hasty words and mean nothing. He won’t kill you. It’s not you he’ll kill!”
“He’d kill me first of all, like a fly. But even more than that, I’m afraid I’ll be taken for his accomplice when he does something crazy to his father.”
“Why should you be taken for an accomplice?”
“They’ll think I’m an accomplice, because I told him the signals, which were a great secret.”
“What signals? Who did you tell? Confound you, speak plainly.”

“I am bound to admit,” Smerdyakov drawled with pedantic composure, “that I have a secret with Fyodor Pavlovitch in this business. As you know yourself (if you do know it), for several days now he has locked himself in as soon as night, or even evening, comes on. Lately you’ve been going up to your room early every evening, and yesterday you didn’t come down at all. So perhaps you don’t know how carefully he has begun to lock himself in at night. Even if Grigory Vassilyevitch comes to the door, he won’t open to him until he hears his voice. But Grigory Vassilyevitch doesn’t come, because I am the only one who waits on him in his room now. That is the arrangement he made himself, ever since this to-do with Agrafena Alexandrovna began. But at night, by his orders, I go away to the lodge. So I don’t get to sleep until midnight, but keep watch, getting up and walking about the yard, waiting for Agrafena Alexandrovna to come. For the last few days he has been perfectly frantic, expecting her. His reasoning is that she is afraid of Dmitri Fyodorovitch (Mitya, as he calls him), ‘and so,’ says he, ‘she’ll come the back way, late at night, to me. You look out for her,’ says he, ‘until midnight and later. And if she does come, you run up and knock at my door, or at the window from the garden. Knock twice at first, rather gently, and then three times more quickly. Then,’ says he, ‘I shall understand at once that she has come, and I will open the door to you quietly.’ He gave me another signal in case anything unexpected happens. At first, two knocks, and then, after a pause, another one, much louder. Then he will understand that something has suddenly happened and that I must see him, and he will open to me so that I can go and speak to him. That is all in case Agrafena Alexandrovna can’t come herself but sends a message. Besides, Dmitri Fyodorovitch might come too, so I must let him know that he is near. His honor is terribly afraid of Dmitri Fyodorovitch. So even if Agrafena Alexandrovna had come and were locked in with him, and Dmitri Fyodorovitch were to turn up anywhere near at the time, I would be bound to let him know at once, by knocking three times. So the first signal, of five knocks, means Agrafena Alexandrovna has come, while the second signal, of three knocks, means ‘something important to tell you.’ His honor has shown them to me several times and explained them. And since no one in the whole universe knows of these signals but myself and his honor, he would open the door without the slightest hesitation and without calling out (he is terribly afraid of calling out aloud). Well, those signals are known to Dmitri Fyodorovitch too, now.”
“How does he know them? Did you tell him? How dared you tell him?”

“I did it out of fright. How could I dare to keep it back from him? Dmitri Fyodorovitch kept pressing me every day: ‘You are deceiving me, you are hiding something from me! I’ll break both your legs for you.’ So I told him those secret signals, so that he would see my slavish devotion and be satisfied that I was not deceiving him but telling him all I could.”
“If you think he’ll use those signals and try to get in, don’t let him in.”
“But if I’m laid up with a fit, how can I stop him coming in then—even if I dared stop him, knowing how desperate he is?”
“Damn it! How can you be so sure you’re going to have a fit, confound you? Are you laughing at me?”
“How could I dare laugh at you? I’m in no laughing mood, with this fear on me. I feel I’m going to have a fit. I have a presentiment. Fright alone will bring it on.”
“Confound it! If you’re laid up, Grigory will be on watch. Tell Grigory beforehand; he’ll be sure not to let him in.”

“I would never dare to tell Grigory Vassilyevitch about the signals without my master’s orders. And as for Grigory Vassilyevitch hearing him and not admitting him, he has been ill ever since yesterday, and Marfa Ignatyevna means to give him medicine tomorrow. They’ve just arranged it. It’s a very strange remedy of hers. Marfa Ignatyevna knows of a preparation and always keeps it. It’s a strong thing made from some herb. She has the secret of it, and she always gives it to Grigory Vassilyevitch three times a year, when his lumbago is so bad that he is almost paralyzed by it. Then she takes a towel, wets it with the stuff, and rubs his whole back for half an hour, until it’s quite red and swollen. What’s left in the bottle she gives him to drink, with a special prayer. But not quite all of it, for on such occasions she leaves some for herself and drinks it herself. And since they never take strong drink, I assure you they both drop asleep at once and sleep soundly for a very long time. When Grigory Vassilyevitch wakes up, he is perfectly well after it, but Marfa Ignatyevna always has a headache from it. So if Marfa Ignatyevna carries out her intention tomorrow, they won’t hear anything and hinder Dmitri Fyodorovitch. They’ll be asleep.”

“What a rigmarole! And it all happens at once, as though it were planned. You’ll have a fit and they’ll both be unconscious,” cried Ivan. “But aren’t you trying to arrange it that way?” broke from him suddenly, and he frowned threateningly.
“How could I?... And why should I, when it all depends on Dmitri Fyodorovitch and his plans?... If he means to do anything, he’ll do it. But if not, I won’t be thrusting him on his father.”

“And why should he go to father, especially on the sly, if Agrafena Alexandrovna won’t come at all, as you say yourself?” Ivan went on, turning white with anger. “You say that yourself, and all the time I’ve been here I’ve felt sure it was all just the old man’s fantasy, and the creature won’t come to him. Why should Dmitri break in on him if she doesn’t come? Speak, I want to know what you are thinking!”

“You know yourself why he’ll come. What’s the use of what I think? His honor will come simply because he is in a rage, or perhaps suspicious because of my illness. He’ll dash in, as he did yesterday, too impatient to wait, to search the rooms and see whether she has slipped past him on the sly. He is also perfectly well aware that Fyodor Pavlovitch has a big envelope with three thousand roubles in it, tied up with ribbon and sealed with three seals. On it is written in his own hand, ‘To my angel Grushenka, if she will come,’ and three days later he added, ‘for my little chicken.’ There’s no knowing what that might lead to.”

“Nonsense!” cried Ivan, almost beside himself. “Dmitri won’t come to steal money and kill my father to get it. He might have killed him yesterday over Grushenka, like the frantic, savage fool he is, but he won’t steal.”

“He is in very great need of money now—the greatest need, Ivan Fyodorovitch. You don’t know how badly he needs it,” Smerdyakov explained, with perfect composure and remarkable distinctness. “He regards that three thousand as his own, too. He said so to me himself. ‘My father still owes me just three thousand,’ he said. And besides that, consider, Ivan Fyodorovitch, something else that is perfectly true. It’s as good as certain, so to say, that Agrafena Alexandrovna will force him to marry her, if only she cares to—the master himself, I mean, Fyodor Pavlovitch—and of course she may care to. All I’ve said is that she won’t come, but maybe she’s after more than that—I mean to be mistress here. I know myself that Samsonov, her merchant, was laughing with her about it, telling her quite openly that it would not be at all a stupid thing to do. And she has plenty of sense. She wouldn’t marry a beggar like Dmitri Fyodorovitch. So, taking that into consideration, Ivan Fyodorovitch, reflect that then neither Dmitri Fyodorovitch nor yourself and your brother Alexey Fyodorovitch would have anything after the master’s death, not a rouble, for Agrafena Alexandrovna would marry him simply to get hold of the whole lot, all the money there is. But if your father were to die now, there’d be some forty thousand for certain, even for Dmitri Fyodorovitch, whom he hates so, for he has made no will.... Dmitri Fyodorovitch knows all that very well.”
A kind of shudder crossed Ivan’s face. He suddenly flushed.

“Then why on earth,” he suddenly interrupted Smerdyakov, “do you advise me to go to Tchermashnya? What did you mean by that? If I go away, you see what will happen here.” Ivan was breathing with difficulty.
“Precisely so,” said Smerdyakov, softly and reasonably, though watching Ivan intently.
“What do you mean, ‘precisely so’?” Ivan demanded, with a menacing light in his eyes, barely restraining himself.

“I spoke because I felt sorry for you. If I were in your place, I would simply throw it all up ... rather than stay on in such a position,” answered Smerdyakov, looking at Ivan’s flashing eyes with the most candid air. They were both silent.

“You seem to be a perfect idiot, and what’s more ... an awful scoundrel, too.” Ivan suddenly rose from the bench. He was about to go straight through the gate, but he stopped short and turned to Smerdyakov. Something strange followed. In a sudden fit of rage, Ivan bit his lip, clenched his fists, and in another moment would have flung himself on Smerdyakov. Smerdyakov noticed it at the same moment, started, and shrank back. But the moment passed without harm to Smerdyakov, and Ivan turned in silence, apparently in perplexity, to the gate.

“I am going away to Moscow tomorrow, if you care to know—early tomorrow morning. That’s all!” he said suddenly, aloud and angrily. Afterwards he wondered himself what need there had been to say this to Smerdyakov just then.
“That’s the best thing you can do,” he responded, as though he had expected to hear it; “except that you can always be telegraphed for from Moscow, if anything should happen here.”

Ivan stopped again and turned quickly to Smerdyakov. But a change had come over him, too. All his familiarity and carelessness had completely disappeared. His face showed attention and expectation, intent but timid and cringing.
“Haven’t you something more to say—something to add?” could be read in the intent gaze he fixed on Ivan.
“And couldn’t I be sent for from Tchermashnya, too, if anything happened?” Ivan suddenly shouted, raising his voice for some unknown reason.
“From Tchermashnya, too ... you could be sent for,” Smerdyakov muttered, almost in a whisper, looking disconcerted but gazing intently into Ivan’s eyes.
“Only Moscow is farther and Tchermashnya is nearer. Is it to save me the fare, or to save me going so far out of my way, that you insist on Tchermashnya?”

“Precisely so ...” muttered Smerdyakov, in a breaking voice. He looked at Ivan with a revolting smile and again got ready to draw back. But to his astonishment Ivan broke into a laugh and went through the gate still laughing. Anyone who had seen his face at that moment would have known he was not laughing from lightness of heart, and he could not have explained himself what he was feeling at that instant. He moved and walked as though in a nervous frenzy.
